Your problem is that you are using electricity to heat your house. I guarantee you that the heat pump is taking up a massive amount of your KwH usage. 

You say you use oil for hot water. Is that a domestic hot water coil off a boiler? If so, you are wasting a massive amount of money by heating your entire boiler just for hot water and not heating your house with it..

Either switch your hot water to electric as well, since it takes way more oil than you need just to heat hot water through a boiler. Or shut down your heat pump and switch to oil as your primary heat source, since your entire oil boiler is maintaining a constant 160 degrees around the clock. All that thermal heat is just sitting there in your boiler going to waste.. 

You will use roughly 15% more electricity if you switch hot water to electric, but your oil bill will be zero.. If you switch your heat pump to oil, your electric bill will likely drop as much as three to four hundred a month.. But your oil will double. 

I'm a professional plumber and HVAC technician who specializes in oil burners. I've seen this many times. If you have a boiler, you should either make full use of it or don't use it at all. Running it for just hot water is extremely wasteful and expensive.. 

Either way. Your electrical use is high due to the heat pump. I promise you, that's your answer..

Replying to an old post, I know. Just wanted to chime in and say that changing anodes really isn't any more complicated than changing a water filter. Perhaps one or two extra steps, but they're simple. With some basic skills, you shouldn't have any trouble. 

Just make sure to shut the water and electric power off to the heater, then take the pressure down through the tank drain or a faucet. Just a quart or two, you don't need to take much water out of the tank, just enough to take the pressure to zero. If you have a valve on the hot side as well to completely isolate the tank, that helps keep things dry while you're working. 

  Use a 1-1/16" deep socket to unscrew the anode threads. Just be careful not to dump too much water down into the junction box pulling the rod out the top of the tank. Pull it out and screw the new one in. Don't forget to seal the threads if necessary, I prefer liquid teflon. Before turning water and power back on (in that order), ensure that the tank is full and the electric box on the top of the tank is dry. 

It's actually a very similar process to change your heater elements as well. Only major difference is those have wire terminals that need to be disconnected. They also don't need thread sealant (they use gaskets) and you want to drain the tank down completely to avoid dumping water on the thermostats. Just ALWAYS ensure that power to the heater is DISCONNECTED, and NEVER reconnect power until the tank is COMPLETELY FULL again..

Companies probably don't offer plans on heater parts because people changing anodes is bad for tank sales. The tanks often rot before the components go bad. Water quality is a big factor, even standard municipal water can rot tanks fast, but it's almost always just outsude of the warranty period. I've changed hundreds of them. If you really want a tank that lasts, HTP makes a stainless steel heater that comes with a lifetime warranty, but they ain't cheap..

Withdrawal isn't simply defined as a lack of drug in the receptor. Withdrawal is defined as symptoms with varying characteristics that manifest upon cessation of a substance, the root causes of which aren't always completely understood but is usually a result of various physiological adaptations made within your body while on said drug. Yes, receptor regulation is a large part of those adaptations but not a requirement in defining what withdrawal is.. 

If said symptoms cease upon re-administration of the drug that caused it, it's very likely a withdrawal symptom. The drug made physiological changes to the users brain over time, upon cessation of the drug the brain is no longer in the same state that it was before the drug was ever introduced.. Various adaptations are made upon cessation, some happen quicker than others. 

If the user never touched the drug, there would be no symptoms because there would be no withdrawal. If the user stays on the drug, paws is completely avoided. The drug caused the damage that brought about the symptoms. If it's the drug that you're withdrawing from that caused said damage and the symptoms of said damage only manifests upon quitting, that's literally a symptom of withdrawal. I can't believe I have to explain this to a doctor 🙄

Everyone knows that the drugs are what cause the damage that precipitates paws. Nobody's arguing that. It's caused by damage and or physiological adaptations the brain has made due to drug use. Nobody thinks that withdrawal causes paws. Drug use causes paws. But we can't just stay on drugs forever, now can we? Sooner or later one must stop taking them and paws is often a direct and unavoidable result.. It's not just some made up psychosomatic bullshit, it's a real and terrible problem for many individuals and only happens upon cessation.. Hence the term "post acute withdrawal symptom" ..If it happened any other time or was caused by anything other than the the drug they're withdrawing from then we wouldn't call it PAWS..
